node.label: Gerda Lerner
node.date_label: “The Lady and the Mill Girl” (1969) · “Placing Women in History” (1975) · The Majority Finds Its Past (1979) · The Creation of Patriarchy (1986) · The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993)
node.description: In The Creation of Patriarchy (1986), Lerner argued that male dominance was made through historical changes in control over women’s sexuality and reproduction, property, law and religious symbols, rather than being biologically inevitable. As Virginia Hunter’s 1988 review observed, she reworked Engels’s historical account of the family together with Lévi-Strauss’s account of the exchange of women. Lerner later explained that she reversed Engels’s causal sequence by placing gender oppression before class oppression. Her essays include “The Lady and the Mill Girl: Changes in the Status of Women in the Age of Jackson” (1969) and “Placing Women in History: Definitions and Challenges” (1975). The Majority Finds Its Past (1979) made recovering women’s agency and rethinking historical categories a programme for women’s history, with differences of class, race, ethnicity and culture central to interpretation. Her documentary collection Black Women in White America (1972) supplied sources for researching African American women, while graduate programmes at Sarah Lawrence and Wisconsin helped train historians in the field. Her large explanatory claims also drew criticism: Virginia Hunter’s 1988 review welcomed the theoretical challenge but argued that Lerner misread the Greek sources on slavery, relied on laws to the exclusion of other evidence, and drew a developmental continuum that was “all too neat.” Linda Gordon’s memorial identified tensions between materialist explanations and Lerner’s emphasis on women’s exclusion from education and knowledge of their past. The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993) extended her inquiry to the barriers to women’s intellectual authority and the ways women challenged them.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Grimké Sisters from South Carolina (1967; revised edition 2004); Black Women in White America: A Documentary History (editor, 1972); The Female Experience: An American Documentary (1976); The Majority Finds Its Past: Placing Women in History (1979; reissue with Linda K. Kerber foreword 2005); The Creation of Patriarchy (1986; author page displays 1987 edition); The Creation of Feminist Consciousness: From the Middle Ages to Eighteen-Seventy (1993); Why History Matters: Life and Thought (1997).
node.scope_note: Selected primary retrospective passages in Lerner’s 2005 lecture and Kerber’s 2020 lecture read; Lerner’s 1988 essay prose, Hunter’s 1988 review and Gordon’s undated memorial read. Statistical tables not audited. Monographs known through author and publisher descriptions, retrospective accounts and the named reviewer; complete book bodies, the 1980 symposium and the 2003 discussion remain unread. The Lévi-Strauss relationship is mediated through Hunter.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Life of Learning (2005), Lerner identifies reading Beard’s Woman as Force in History (1946) as a formative source for treating women as historical agents, including differences and conflicts among women.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lerner, printed 12–13 (PDF pages 20–21), paragraph beginning “I had first read Mary Beard’s”: calls Beard her “principal mentor” as a historian while explicitly saying they never met. She retains reservations about Beard and adapts rather than simply repeats the argument. Woman as Force in History was not freshly read; its original 1946 date is independently retained in the existing Beard node and source record.
proposed_edges.map_label: Beard’s agency argument and intellectual mentorship

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Life of Learning (2005), Lerner recalls developing the interdisciplinary foundation course for Sarah Lawrence’s women’s-history MA programme with Joan Kelly-Gadol, Sherry Ortner and Eva Kollisch after establishing the programme in 1972.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lerner, printed 14 (PDF page 22), paragraph beginning “In 1972 I established”: the course was “team-taught” by all four named teachers and combined lectures, seminars, tutorials and student research. Kerber and Kessler-Harris (2013), paragraph beginning “Working with Renaissance historian Joan Kelly,” independently identifies programme development with Kelly. Kelly-Gadol is the queued joan_kelly identity. This is collaboration, not intellectual descent or a claim that two people alone taught the course. Original course materials unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Joint development and teaching of women’s history

proposed_edges.relationship: Hunter’s 1988 review identifies Lévi-Strauss’s account of the exchange of women as a theoretical resource that Lerner reworks, alongside Engels, in The Creation of Patriarchy (1986).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hunter, p. 240, paragraphs beginning “There is more” and “What role”: names Lévi-Strauss and describes the synthesis with Engels as “she has wed the two.” Mediated evidence from a substantive named reader. Neither Lerner’s monograph nor Lévi-Strauss’s relevant text was read here; Hunter does not identify a particular Lévi-Strauss edition. No unqualified adoption, exclusive influence or agreement with all structuralism is asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Exchange of women reworked in a historical explanation

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Life of Learning (2020), Kerber credits Lerner’s perspective and pioneering work with providing later professional mentorship after Hofstadter’s death.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kerber’s own lecture, printed 9 (PDF page 21), paragraph beginning “Many people find their professional mentors”: explicitly assigns Lerner that role and describes her work as “a lodestar.” Kerber says she did not send Lerner drafts; no manuscript supervision or doctoral supervision is claimed. The full corpus of either historian’s work remains unread. Separate from the existing Hofstadter-to-Kerber edge_2234, whose evidence already mentions this later relationship but does not represent it as a Lerner edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her undated memorial “Biography,” Gordon identifies herself as Lerner’s co-director of the University of Wisconsin women’s-history programme until Lerner retired, and recalls working with her daily.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gordon, paragraphs beginning “At Wisconsin she took the job” and “I had the privilege,” and the author identification immediately after her signature: explicit “co-director” credit until Lerner retired. The text dates Gordon’s recruitment to 1984, but its sixteen-year recollection is not used to construct a duration. No publication date is displayed. Co-direction and pedagogical work, not employment alone, support this undirected collaboration. Programme records and teaching materials unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner calls for challenging what she regards as ahistoricity in influential theories of Simone de Beauvoir.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Final theoretical-priorities section, paragraph beginning “We could, to begin with”: explicitly names Beauvoir alongside broader theoretical currents and uses “ahistoricity.” It is Lerner’s programmatic criticism, not an independently demonstrated defect in Beauvoir. No particular Beauvoir work is named, so The Second Sex is not silently supplied; Beauvoir’s works remain unread. The endpoint is another person in this run.
proposed_edges.map_label: Calls for historically contextualizing Beauvoir’s theory

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner treats Smith-Rosenberg’s insights into women’s homoerotic relationships as a resource for further research, while questioning whether she has said the last word and calling for tests against other primary sources.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the AHA article, paragraph beginning “On the subject of differences.” Lerner asks whether Smith-Rosenberg has said the last word, then proposes testing her insights against other sources. Retain the incoming resource classification but make its questioning explicit; this is neither blanket acceptance nor an assertion that Lerner completed such a test. No particular Smith-Rosenberg title is identified in this passage.
proposed_edges.map_label: Insights questioned and proposed for testing

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner proposes documentary recovery, interpretation from women’s perspectives, comparison among women and reconstruction of historical concepts as a programme for women’s history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paragraphs beginning “These fall into four categories,” “Please notice,” and “The third point”: first priority is “Restoring and documenting the female past”; she opposes premature incorporation into an unchanged general narrative and makes differences among women analytically central. The essay is a situated intervention based on a 1987 paper; its statistical tables were not audited. Existing women/identity roster contexts and group edge_090 are retained. The new personal edge identifies Lerner’s own contribution without making her the field’s sole founder.
proposed_edges.map_label: Recovery, differences and a revised historical framework

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Priorities and Challenges in Women’s History Research” (1988), Lerner proposes comparing women across class and race and relating changing gender definitions to changing economic and social conditions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning “For example, a comparison” explicitly links comparative work to gender and class formation; paragraph beginning “We might ask some basic transforming questions” asks about “changing gender definitions” and economic and social conditions. This is an analytic programme, not evidence that Lerner accepted every later version of gender history. Gordon’s memorial separately records her misgivings about a turn that displaced women as collective subjects. Group edge_091 already connects women’s history to gender history; this proposal records the named author’s distinct intervention.
proposed_edges.map_label: Historically situated gender, class and race analysis

proposed_edges.relationship: Black Women in White America: A Documentary History (1972) assembled primary sources and a bibliographic guide for researching African American women; Lerner’s A Life of Learning (2005) describes its role in developing that scholarship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lerner, printed 15–16 (PDF pages 23–24), paragraphs beginning “During my research on this book” and “I am happy to say”: describes the source collection and bibliographic essay. Gordon’s memorial, paragraphs beginning “She devoted the rest of her life” and “It was her second book,” corroborates its research use. The anthology itself is unread. This is a contribution within Black history, not the origin of Black history or a priority claim over earlier Black scholars. Existing black node and its independent roots inspected.
proposed_edges.map_label: Documentary resources for African American women’s history

proposed_edges.relationship: Discussing The Creation of Patriarchy (1986) and The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993) in her undated “Biography,” Gordon identifies tension between their Marxist and radical-feminist explanations, calling the account of exclusion from education and historical knowledge non-materialist.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gordon, paragraph beginning “To do this massive study”: says the “two theoretical strands argue with each other” and calls the education-and-knowledge explanation “a most non-materialist claim.” The following paragraph connects this to Lerner’s advocacy of women’s history. A sympathetic but specific critical reading, not wholesale rejection. Both monographs remain unread; no original date is supplied for the undated memorial. Separate argument from the co-direction relationship.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gordon on competing explanations of subordination

proposed_edges.relationship: In Women, Race & Class (1981), Angela Y. Davis drew upon the analysis of rape in Gerda Lerner’s Black Women in White America (1972), crediting Lerner with examining racism and sexism together in Black women’s experiences.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed Google Books search extract of Davis’s body paragraph on p. 174. Davis explicitly identifies Lerner as the author of the passage under discussion and singles out her combined analysis of racism and sexism in writing about rape. Also read the 1983 preview’s search extract of p. 266, note 4, identifying Lerner’s Black Women in White America, p. 193 (https://books.google.com/books?jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=Lerner&vid=iCknYRPikTEC). The complete p. 174 was restricted and remains unread; this proposal rests on the displayed body extract and identifying note, not a full-chapter reading. It records a specific use, not a general intellectual debt or agreement with Lerner’s entire collection. Original publication in 1981 is confirmed by the Google Books record for the Random House edition (https://books.google.com/books/about/Women_Race_Class.html?id=lye5AAAAIAAJ); 2011 and 1983 are the consulted reprint dates.
proposed_edges.map_label: Davis draws on Lerner’s analysis of racism, sexism and rape

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1995 review of Gerda Lerner’s The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993), Lynn Hunt contrasted Lerner’s broad historical synthesis with the small-scale social history and microhistory then prevalent among historians.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s metadata and visually read its first-page preview, printed p. 675. The top of that page concludes a different review; Hunt’s review begins below the bibliographical heading for Lerner’s book. Hunt contrasts contemporary historians’ narrowing scales with Lerner’s two-volume synthesis and asks whether the book signals renewed grand synthesis or calls for caution about generalization. Only p. 675 was available; pp. 676–677 remain unread. The comparison classification records the review and this specific discussion of scale; it does not attribute a final favorable or unfavorable verdict to Hunt. No directed influence or definite criticism is inferred from the opening questions.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hunt reviews Lerner’s return to broad historical synthesis
